summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations: the colonial-era ban was abolished in 1951, and no statute on the books criminalises gender expression as such. That baseline does not translate into safety. Human Rights Watch reported in June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait substitute public-morality and debauchery provisions for formal criminalisation, using them to harass LGBT people legally.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change official gender markers, transgender people cannot. The Court of Cassation's ruling in Case No. 2092/2014 allowed a plaintiff born in 1977 to change name and gender from male to female in official records after hormone therapy and surgery undertaken in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically; the court justified the change by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex rather than recognising a trans identity.

Gender-affirming surgery is permitted for intersex people and criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law No. 25 of 2018, with penalties reaching ten years' imprisonment; providers face liability under the same medical-liability framework. Care that cannot be obtained at home must therefore be sought abroad.

The operating environment has tightened. A cybercrime law enacted in 2023 criminalises online speech on grounds of inciting immorality and undermines free speech and privacy, and Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records the arrest and harassment of peaceful dissidents and journalists under vague laws alongside intrusive digital surveillance. In December 2023 Human Rights Watch documented a coordinated crackdown in which authorities targeted LGBT rights activists, officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users circulated their photographs with messages inciting violence, and directors of two LGBT organisations described official intimidation.

CAIRO 52's Jordan profile reports a notable rise in the targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, working through Ottoman- and British-era morality provisions, and states that security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activity, pushing transgender and queer people to leave. New legislation further curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access, and intersex people can change legal gender markers while transgender people cannot.
tangentialFactors:
The absence of explicit criminalisation is regional rather than distinctive: Human Rights Watch grouped Jordan with Egypt and Kuwait in 2024 as jurisdictions where same-sex relations are not formally banned yet are pursued through morality and debauchery provisions. The practical difference for a visitor lies in which statute an officer reaches for, not whether conduct is lawful on paper.

Restrictions on civic space extend beyond LGBT issues. The 2023 cybercrime law and the arrests of dissidents and journalists documented in the World Report 2024 form a general environment of online surveillance and vague-law enforcement, so digital caution applies to any visitor whose messages touch sexuality or gender.

Regional LGBT movements continue to organise despite repression, according to Human Rights Watch's 2018 report on activism across the Middle East and North Africa, whose annex sets out the statutes used against same-sex conduct and gender expression, including in Jordan. Organisational presence therefore exists, but under conditions of documented intimidation rather than protected assembly.
localsOnly:
Residents have no administrative route to change a gender marker on the basis of a transgender identity; the available route runs through intersex classification, as in Case No. 2092/2014. People who have transitioned abroad remain unable to reflect that status in Jordanian records.

Providers of gender-affirming surgery face criminal liability under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law No. 25 of 2018 where the patient is transgender, which effectively removes domestic surgical care from residents as well as visitors.

Community organisations have been coerced into closing, and LGBT activists have been targeted by officials through online smears and intimidation of organisational directors. Residents operating in this space carry exposure that does not fall away when they are at home.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory attributes a ten-year maximum penalty for sex reassignment to Jordanian legislation in the context of the 2014 case analysis, while the statutory citation supplied for the current ban is Article 8 of the 2018 Medical and Health Liability Law. Whether the ten-year figure derives from the earlier statute, from the 2018 law, or from both is unresolved in these sources.

OutRight International's profile, updated 12 March 2026, states that marker changes are allowed 'in some cases' without specifying the criteria, which sits uneasily with the intersex-only reading given by CAIRO 52. The scope of any exception beyond intersex classification is not sourced here.

Enforcement frequency is not established: the sources document a 2023 crackdown, coerced closures and a reported rise in targeting, but give no figures on arrests, prosecutions or convictions under morality provisions, and no data on violence against trans visitors specifically. Whether the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling binds lower courts as precedent is also not addressed.
